sample_note: Stromboli: highest point about 926 m, crater terrace at about 700–750 m, base about 2,000 m below sea level, explosions minutes to hours apart, strongest paroxysms 1919, 1930, 2003, 2019, ages of about 200,000 and 85,000 years. Mount Pinatubo (read 2026-11-17): HazardHunterPH monitoring page: Alert Level 0, “No eruption in foreseeable future”. Cotopaxi (read 2026-11-17): IG-EPN profile: 5,897 m, 45 km SE of Quito and 35 km NE of Latacunga, slopes up to 35°, base about 20 km, crater about 800 by 650 m, five eruptive periods since 1532, eruptions of 2015 and of October 2022 to July 2023, first seismic station 1976, more than 300,000 people in lahar zones. Reports list: newest report 21 Oct 2026, internal and surface activity low and unchanged; no ash emissions since July 2023. 1877 article: pyroclastic flows on 26 Jun 1877 melted part of the glacier; lahars reached Latacunga in a little over 30 minutes, the Chillos Valley in under an hour, the mouth of the Esmeraldas in about 18 hours; ash nearly 2 cm at Machachi, 6 mm in Quito. Sakurajima (read 2026-11-17): JMA catalogue chapter: Kitadake 1,117 m and Minamidake 1,060 m; peninsula 12.2 by 9.5 km on the southern rim of the Aira caldera (17 by 23 km); an island until lava closed the Seto strait on 29 Jan 1914; 1914 eruption from about 10:00 on 12 Jan, M 7.1 earthquake at 18:29, 1.58 km3 of magma, 58 killed and 112 injured, about 2,140 buildings buried or burnt; 1779 eruption 1.86 km3 and over 150 killed; 474 summit explosions in 1985, 994 at the Showa crater in 2011; alert levels since 1 Dec 2007; Kagoshima City 608,219 residents and the Sakurajima area 5,262 (2011). RSN paper: 15 km2 laid waste in three days in 1968, 78 killed, 230 km2 affected. OVSICORI bulletin of 18 Oct 2024: 1,755 m, activity level “Calma”. sample_note: Mauna Loa: summit 4,169 m (13,679 ft), threat potential very high, flanks about 5,000 m further down to the sea floor, sea floor pressed down about 8,000 m, more than 17,000 m base to summit, 34 eruptions since 1843, three since 1950, 38 years quiet from 1984 to 2022, first lava 0.6 to 1 million years ago, above the sea about 300,000 years ago, area about 5,100 km2, volume at least 75,000 km3, caldera 5 by 3.2 km, 2022 flows 19 km long and 2.8 km short of the highway. All five pages answer 200. Mount St. Helens (17 Nov 2026): summit 9,677 ft before and 8,363 ft after May 18, 1980; crater 1.2 by 1.8 miles and 2,084 ft deep; 57 deaths; landslide 0.67 cubic miles; blast 230 square miles; 2004–08 dome about 92 million m3; history about 300,000 years. All three pages answer 200. Kilauea (read 2026-11-17): summit 1,222 m (4,009 ft); eruption since 23 Dec 2024, episode 56 on 5 Nov 2026; tallest fountain 540 m (1,770 ft) in episode 43 on 10 Mar 2026; Halemaʻumaʻu floor 1,023 m before and 518 m after the 2018 collapse, lava surface 1,007 m on 30 Jun 2026; 2018: 35.5 sq km covered, 875 acres of new land, 62 collapses. Mount Pinatubo (read 2026-11-17): Fact Sheet 113-97: more than 1 cubic mile (5 km3) erupted on 15 Jun 1991, ash cloud 22 miles (35 km) high, deposits up to 660 ft (200 m) thick, caldera 1.6 miles (2.5 km) across, nearly 20 million tons of SO2, about 1°F (0.5°C) of cooling 1991–93, at least 5,000 lives and $250 million saved. Fire and Mud: former summit 1,745 m; climactic eruption from 13:42 for about 9 hours; flows 12–16 km; evacuations of about 5,000, then 25,000, then at least 58,000 people; about 14,500 left Clark Air Base on 10 Jun; six earlier eruptive periods, the first more than 35,000 years ago and about five times the size of 1991; caldera more than 650 m deep. 2016 feature: more than 840 deaths, at least 17 jets damaged, about $100 million. Mount Pelee (read 2026-11-17, from the pages’ text in search results): Volcano Watch “Dual volcanic tragedies in the Caribbean led to founding of HVO”: St. Pierre destroyed on 8 May 1902 in 2–3 minutes, 28,000 deaths, a day after Soufrière on St. Vincent (2,000 deaths) 150 km away; FAQ: a pyroclastic flow (“nuée ardente”) killed nearly 30,000; Volcano Watch on Frank Perret: the 1929–32 eruption built a lava dome whose collapses fed pyroclastic flows.
notes: The overview page gives the summit as 4,169 m, the FAQ as about 4,170 m: the page prints the overview figure. The FAQ says seven flows threatened Hilo and lists eight, and gives three different distances for the 1984 flow: the page prints no count and uses the list’s distance to Komohana Street. Mount St. Helens: USGS counts 57 deaths for May 18, 1980 and NOAA’s database lists 61; the page prints both and leads with USGS. Kilauea: the overview gives the summit as 1,222 m while the FAQ lists the Uēkahuna overlook on the rim at 1,247 m: the page prints both and says which is which. The Eruption Information page says the 2020–2023 eruptions filled about 410 m to an elevation of 910 m, which does not add up from 518 m: the page prints the elevations only. USGS calls its 2026 crater figures preliminary; the page says so. Episode counts change about every 11 days: the page gives them with their dates. Counts of buildings lost in 2018 differ between USGS pages (more than 700 structures, 716 dwellings, more than 724 structures): the page uses the 2018 science page. The quick-facts box still says the most recent eruption was June 2024. Mount Pinatubo: the fact sheet’s web page (pubs.usgs.gov/fs/1997/fs113-97/) did not answer on 2026-11-17; the PDF under fs/old.1997/ did, and the page links that. Deaths: the 1996 overview says 200 to 300 during the eruption, the 2016 feature more than 840, NOAA 800: the page prints the 2016 figure and NOAA’s. Height of the ash cloud: 22 miles (35 km) in the fact sheet, 28 miles (40 km) in the 2016 feature: the page uses the fact sheet. SO2: nearly 20 million tons in the fact sheet, about 17 Mt in the overview: the page uses the fact sheet. The summit loss of 259 m is calculated from USGS’s 1,745 m and the Smithsonian’s 1,486 m; the Smithsonian’s own texts give about 300 m in one place and 145 m in another. Mount Pelee: USGS pages give 28,000, “nearly 30,000”, 30,000 (29,025) and “26,000 inhabitants” for the dead of 1902; NOAA lists 28,000 for 8 May and 1,500 for 30 Aug: the page prints USGS’s 28,000 and “nearly 30,000” and NOAA’s figures. The three USGS pages were read as search-result text, not fetched whole.
